## Kabah excursions: combining two Maya cities in Yucatán

[Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/) lies on the Yucatán Peninsula in the Puuc archaeological region. The ancient city is famous for the Temple of the Masks, whose façade is covered with repeated depictions of the rain god Chaac, and a great stone arch. These details offer a noticeably different architectural experience from nearby [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/).

We offer the [Uxmal, Kabah and Cenote Swimming excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/). It combines **2 archaeological complexes and a freshwater cenote**. Kabah is one stop on the route, so plan for the entire day's duration rather than several hours solely at the Temple of the Masks.

## Why visit Kabah after Uxmal?

Uxmal is known for the Pyramid of the Magician, Governor's Palace and other buildings showcasing Maya architectural skill. Kabah is particularly striking for its decorative façades: repeated masks, carvings and stone ornaments. Seeing the two sites side by side helps you recognize shared elements of the Puuc style as well as differences in their decoration.

Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) describes Kabah as an archaeological site near the road through Santa Elena and part of the Puuc region's group of ancient settlements. Visiting hours, building conservation and access rules apply. Confirm them for your travel date, particularly when planning two archaeological zones in a single day.

The [Kabah guide](/mexico/place/kabah/) describes its history and principal monuments. The practical excursion question is different: how much time to allocate to each site and how to spend the rest of the day.

## What the Ada Tours excursion includes

The [Uxmal, Kabah and Cenote Swimming trip](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) lasts **8–9 hours**, begins at approximately 9:00–9:30 and includes a group transfer, a certified English- and Spanish-speaking guide and **admission tickets to both archaeological complexes and the cenote**. Meals, tips and personal expenses are explicitly excluded.

Travelers first explore Uxmal, then Kabah, with a final stop at a cenote where swimming is possible. Confirm the exact swimming location for the chosen date: the itinerary does not name a particular cenote.

The excursion suits lovers of ancient architecture who want a nature stop alongside historic sites. For travelers only interested in Uxmal, another product is available: [Uxmal and Cenote](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/), which does not include a visit to Kabah.

## Visiting Kabah from Mérida: arranging the day

[Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) is a convenient base for excursions across western Yucatán. You can stay overnight and dedicate a full day to Uxmal and Kabah. The itinerary combines drives with walks around exposed archaeological sites, where water, a hat, sun protection and closed-toe shoes are useful in hot weather.

If you also plan to see [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/) or more distant parts of Yucatán, do not automatically add them to this excursion: the approved 8–9-hour program already has three substantial stages.

## Choosing between Kabah and other excursions

| Option | Main difference |
|---|---|
| Uxmal + Kabah | Two Maya archaeological sites |
| Uxmal + cenote | One archaeological site |

The Kabah option is better for comparing decorative architecture. The option with fewer archaeological stops, [Uxmal and Cenote](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/), focuses on one historic city. Compare the actual stated durations of the excursions, rather than assuming that fewer stops always make a tour shorter.

For other destinations, explore the [Mexico excursions catalog](/mexico/excursion/). It lets you compare different types of trips around Yucatán and the country's other regions without confusing their geography.

## Frequently asked questions about Kabah excursions

### Can Kabah and Uxmal be visited in one day?

Yes. We offer an [8–9-hour excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) including both archaeological complexes and a cenote.

### Are admission tickets included?

Admission to Uxmal, Kabah and the cenote is included. Meals and personal expenses are paid separately.

### Where is the most convenient place to depart for Kabah?

[Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) is a convenient base for exploring western Yucatán. Confirm the group transfer's exact pickup point when booking.

### Does the cenote cost extra?

Cenote admission is included in the excursion price. Any additional personal expenses outside the stated inclusions are paid separately.

## Excursions in and from Mérida: choosing a Yucatán itinerary

[Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) is the capital of the Mexican state of Yucatán and a convenient base for exploring historic Maya cities. You can spend a few hours among colonial buildings, then take a separate trip to archaeological sites or natural cenotes the following day.

Ada Tours offers both city and countryside excursions associated with Mérida. It is important to distinguish **a walking tour**, a full-day archaeological visit and a journey to natural pools: the same departure city does not imply the same physical demands or price.

## Walking tour of the historic center

The [Mérida Historic Center Walking Tour](/mexico/merida/merida-historic-centre-walking-tour/) lasts **2.5–3 hours**. It passes San Ildefonso Cathedral, Zócalo Square, historic streets and Paseo de Montejo with its European-influenced mansions.

A certified English- and Spanish-speaking guide conducts the tour. The excursion can begin **at 13:00, 16:00 or 18:00**. Food, tips and personal expenses are not included in the stated services.

It works well on arrival day if your schedule allows, or as a standalone introduction to the city. It provides an overview of Mérida's urban history but does not replace visiting Maya pyramids or cenotes.

## Uxmal and Kabah: an archaeological day

From Mérida, you can dedicate a separate day to [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) and [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/). Both sites belong to the Puuc architectural tradition. Uxmal is known for its large structures and monumental squares, while Kabah features carved façades and repeated images of the rain god Chaac.

The [Uxmal, Kabah and Cenote Swimming excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) takes **8–9 hours**. It includes a group transfer, certified bilingual guide and admission tickets to both archaeological sites and the cenote. Meals are excluded.

There is also [Uxmal and Cenote](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-cenote-tour/), a separate excursion without a scheduled visit to Kabah. Choose according to whether you want to compare two Maya cities or focus on Uxmal and swimming.

## Santa Bárbara cenotes: a nature excursion

For travelers interested in Yucatán's natural formations, there is the [Magic of the Santa Bárbara Cenotes excursion](/mexico/santa-barbara-cenotes/santa-barbara-cenotes-tour/). It lasts **8 hours**, begins at about 9:00–9:30 and visits several cenotes around Homún.

The program covers three or four cenotes, with transfers between them by bicycle or the traditional transport known as a *truck*. Included are shared transport, admissions and relevant equipment, including a life jacket and means of transport. Meals, tips and personal expenses are paid separately.

Swimming in cenotes differs from a standard pool: lighting, depth and access to the water depend on the particular natural site. Follow the guide's instructions and take your own swimming skills into account.

## How much time to spend in Mérida

| Time available | Practical choice |
|---|---|
| A few hours | Historic center |
| One free day | Archaeology or cenotes |
| Two days or more | City plus an excursion |

If your Yucatán trip includes transfers between [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/) and other towns, Mérida can be a convenient overnight stop. But trying to combine the city walking tour, a full Uxmal–Kabah day and several cenotes within a single day is unrealistic.

Also, do not confuse **Mérida in Mexico** with the city of the same name in Venezuela. All the excursions described here take place in Mexico's Yucatán.

## What to confirm beforehand

For city tours, the start time and guide language matter. For archaeological trips, check the schedule, admission tickets, monument access, group transport and meals. For cenotes, confirm the number of stops, equipment and bathing conditions. Before traveling, verify archaeological-site opening hours with INAH and the actual conditions of the selected excursion.

The [Mexico excursions catalog](/mexico/excursion/) contains further themed options, while the [tours catalog](/mexico/tour/) shows itineraries that include Mérida as a stop. Not every standalone excursion is automatically included in the price of a multi-day tour.

## Frequently asked questions about Mérida excursions

### Which excursion should I choose on my first visit?

For a first introduction to Mérida itself, take the [2.5–3-hour walking tour](/mexico/merida/merida-historic-centre-walking-tour/). If you know the city already and have a full day, choose Uxmal or the cenotes.

### Can Uxmal and Kabah be visited in one day?

Yes. The [Ada Tours excursion](/mexico/uxmal/uxmal-kabah-cenote-tour/) includes both sites and a cenote, with a stated duration of 8–9 hours.

### Is there an excursion just to cenotes?

Yes. [Magic of the Santa Bárbara Cenotes](/mexico/santa-barbara-cenotes/santa-barbara-cenotes-tour/) focuses on the natural pools, with swimming and travel between several cenotes.

### Are meals included in all excursions?

No. Food is paid for separately on the city walking tour, the trip to Uxmal and the cenote excursion. Check each product's conditions individually.

## Mérida in 3 hours: the square, cathedral and Paseo de Montejo

[Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) is the capital of the Mexican state of Yucatán. Colonial buildings and 19th-century streets stand alongside the Maya heritage that remains part of the city's culture. Our walking tour introduces the historic center and its main architectural landmarks.

The program lasts **2.5–3 hours**. Choose a start time of **13:00, 16:00 or 18:00**. A **certified bilingual guide** leads the excursion, with English and Spanish available. Meals, tips and personal expenses are not included.

## Mérida's central square

The historic center is organized around a large square known as **Plaza Grande or the Zócalo**. Administrative and religious buildings stand around it, and the square remains an important part of city life. It helps explain how Spanish town-planning principles were applied to the former Maya settlement of T'ho.

Historic façades survive around the square, including administrative buildings and old mansions. According to Yucatán state's official tourism portal, nearby landmarks include San Ildefonso Cathedral, the Government Palace and Casa de Montejo.

Learning about the buildings and viewing their exteriors does not automatically include entering them: specific interior visits and admission tickets are not separately stated in the excursion inclusions.

## San Ildefonso Cathedral: 16th-century architecture

**San Ildefonso Cathedral** is one of Mérida's most important landmarks. It was built in the second half of the 16th century, using stones from ancient Maya structures for parts of the building. The cathedral thus evokes several periods in the region's history at once: ancient T'ho, colonial Yucatán and modern Mérida.

From outside, the massive stonework, two towers and comparatively austere façade are particularly striking. The guide can explain how the city grew around the cathedral and why it became an important symbol of Mérida.

Interior access depends on opening hours and church services. **The cathedral is part of the sightseeing route, but a separate interior visit is not specified among the included services.**

## Paseo de Montejo: the late-19th-century city

The walk then introduces **Paseo de Montejo**, one of Mérida's best-known boulevards. Its mansions, broad streets and European-influenced façades recall Yucatán's period of economic expansion associated with henequen, a plant whose fibers provided an important industrial material.

The contrast between Paseo de Montejo and the old square reveals how Mérida developed over centuries. Religious and administrative buildings from the colonial period dominate the historic center, while the boulevard features villas and urban architecture from a later era.

Much of the excursion is on foot, so the exact walking distance and pace should suit the participants. In Yucatán's hot climate, the time of day and amount of shade have a significant effect on comfort.

## Preparing for the walk

Wear comfortable shoes, light clothing and sun protection. During hotter months, allow for humidity and short breaks. An evening walk provides different lighting over the squares but does not guarantee attendance at a particular cultural event.

The guide can recommend places to discover Yucatán cuisine, such as local corn-based dishes and traditional ways of preparing meat. **These recommendations do not mean that food is included in the excursion.**

The walking tour is included in the [8-day Mexico Lindo journey](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/), where Mérida is one of the stops en route to Yucatán's archaeological sites.

## Frequently asked questions about Mérida's walking tour

### How long does the tour take?

**2.5–3 hours**, depending on the actual walking pace and agreed stops.

### When can the walk begin?

Three start times are offered: **13:00, 16:00 and 18:00**.

### What languages does the guide speak?

The listing specifies **English and Spanish**. Other languages need separate agreement.

### Is lunch included?

No. Meals, tips and personal expenses are excluded from the price.

### Will we enter the cathedral and other buildings?

The cathedral and historic landmarks are included in the sightseeing route. Interior visits and any required admission tickets must be confirmed separately.

## Tours featuring Mérida's historic walking excursion: two ways to travel

[Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) is a convenient Yucatán stop between Mexico's capital, ancient Maya sites and the Caribbean coast. A walking tour of the historic center introduces the city before excursions to Uxmal or Chichén Itzá. Its own itinerary includes Zócalo Square, San Ildefonso Cathedral, historic buildings and Paseo de Montejo. According to the confirmed description, the [Mérida walking tour](/mexico/merida/merida-historic-centre-walking-tour/) takes **2.5–3 hours**.

This catalog contains {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} including a walk through Mérida's historic center: [Mexico Lindo: 8 Days](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) and [Central America: 8 Countries in 26 Days](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/). Both begin in Mexico City but take different routes after Mérida.

## How the excursion fits into each itinerary

| Tour | Mérida's place in the program |
|---|---|
| [Mexico Lindo](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) | Day 5, beginning a three-night stay |
| [Central America](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) | Day 4, before Chichén Itzá and Cancún |

On **Mexico Lindo**, Mérida serves as the base for exploring Yucatán. Before arriving, travelers visit Mexico City, Teotihuacan, the Basilica of Guadalupe and Xochimilco. On day 5, guests fly from Mexico City to Mérida, receive a transfer and explore the historic center. The following days bring excursions to Uxmal and Kabah, the Santa Bárbara cenotes, and a final day covering [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), a cenote and Valladolid. The trip ends with drop-off on the Riviera Maya. It lasts **8 days and 7 nights**, including 3 nights in Mérida.

On the **26-day Central America tour**, Mérida's walk falls on day 4 after the flight from Mexico City. The very next day, travelers visit a cenote and Chichén Itzá, then continue to Cancún. After Mexico, the journey passes through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. Here Mérida is a brief cultural stop linking different historical periods and regions, rather than a three-day base for Yucatán excursions.

The right choice therefore depends on your travel goals. If you want more time in Yucatán, choose among [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/), particularly the 8-day option. If you dream of visiting several countries, consider [multi-country itineraries](/multi-country/), where the Mérida walk is one of many stops.

## What you will see on the walk

The excursion begins in Mérida's historic district. The central landmarks are **San Ildefonso Cathedral** and Zócalo Square, followed by city streets and **Paseo de Montejo**, a boulevard of mansions with visible European architectural influences. The guide explains the city's development and the cultural connections between Maya heritage and the colonial period.

This is a **2.5–3-hour** walking tour in English or Spanish. Possible starting times are **13:00, 16:00 and 18:00**. Guests arriving by air on the same day should coordinate the walk with their arrival and transfer: the available time slots do not mean every flight connection will automatically fit.

The excursion includes a certified bilingual guide. Meals, tips and personal expenses are excluded from its standalone price. The 26-day itinerary separately specifies English-language guiding, with the actual timing agreed under the tour program. Do not apply the standalone excursion's terms to every other day of the larger journey.

## Linking Mérida with Chichén Itzá and the coast

On both journeys, the cultural walk introduces a broader itinerary through Yucatán. After exploring Mérida, compare how much time is allocated to subsequent sites, rather than judging a journey solely by the number of cities in its title.

[Mexico Lindo](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) allows time for Uxmal, Kabah and the Santa Bárbara cenotes. Its final day connects Chichén Itzá, Valladolid and a transfer to the Caribbean coast. On the [26-day program](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/), the next Mexican stop is Chichén Itzá, followed by Cancún and the Belize stage. Travelers keen on Maya archaeology should therefore compare which monuments the routes cover and the time given to each.

Ada Tours helps coordinate flights, transfers and excursions within the chosen program. When purchasing, check particularly whether the domestic Mexico City–Mérida flight is included. On Mexico Lindo, it is paid for separately; on the 26-day journey, flight conditions depend on the individually agreed program and confirmed travel documents.

## Frequently asked questions about tours with Mérida's walking excursion

### How long does the walk itself last?

**2.5–3 hours**, covering the historic center, Zócalo Square and Paseo de Montejo. This excludes the flight to Mérida and the airport transfer.

### Which tours specifically include Mérida as a guided excursion?

[Mexico Lindo](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/) and [Central America: 8 Countries in 26 Days](/multi-country/tour/central-america-8-countries-26-days/) have a direct link to the canonical walking excursion. Other itineraries may visit Mérida, but that does not establish that they include the same module.

### Do I need an entire separate day for Mérida?

The walking tour itself takes part of a day, but independent planning must account for arrival and subsequent excursions. Mexico Lindo includes 3 nights in Mérida, while the stop on the larger multi-country route is much shorter.

### Is the excursion conducted in Russian?

The excursion's confirmed languages are English and Spanish; the 26-day tour specifies English-language guiding. Russian-speaking service is not listed as included.

## Mexico City and Teotihuacan excursions: choosing a history-focused itinerary

Mexico City and [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) are often combined on a trip through [Mexico](/mexico/), but they are distinct excursion destinations. Mexico City is a vast modern metropolis with colonial buildings, the ruins of Tenochtitlan and museums. Teotihuacan is a separate archaeological site outside the capital, home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon.

The first decision is therefore between **the history of the city** and **a dedicated outing to the pyramids**. Ada Tours offers several routes, and the phrase "Mexico City and Teotihuacan" should not create the impression that every excursion necessarily includes both destinations.

## Historic center and the National Museum of Anthropology

The [Eternal Streets and Cultural Treasures excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-history-anthropology-tour/) lasts **6 hours**. It combines Mexico City's historic center, the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/) and the National Museum of Anthropology. This excursion includes English- and Spanish-speaking guiding, shared transportation and admission to the anthropology museum.

The [Zócalo, Chapultepec and Anthropology Museum excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/) also explores the capital but emphasizes [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/) and museum collections. It includes English-speaking guiding and admission services **according to the chosen program**. Visiting the National Palace depends on public access and cannot be treated as a guaranteed interior stop.

Both tours introduce Mexico City's development from pre-Hispanic times to the modern capital, but differ in their order of stops and the time available for each attraction.

## Teotihuacan and the Guadalupe shrine: a separate day

[Teotihuacan and the Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) is a standalone **10-hour** excursion. It includes the Basilica of Guadalupe complex and a walk through the archaeological site of Teotihuacan, with the Pyramid of the Sun, Pyramid of the Moon and Avenue of the Dead.

The tour includes shared transport, a certified bilingual guide and admission to Teotihuacan. Meals, drinks, tips and personal expenses are excluded. This route suits travelers who want to see an ancient site outside the city rather than spend the entire day in capital-city museums.

INAH notes that exploring the principal parts of Teotihuacan generally takes **several hours**, and visitors must follow the permitted routes. Avoid scheduling a tightly timed evening activity immediately after this lengthy excursion.

## Choosing a route by interest

| Main interest | Suitable format |
|---|---|
| Museums and the Zócalo | Historic center |
| Park and anthropology | Chapultepec |
| Ancient pyramids | Teotihuacan |

If time is limited, dedicate a full excursion day to your highest priority. With a longer stay, you can devote one day to the [Teotihuacan archaeological site](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and another to [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/), including museums and squares.

The difference is substantial: a museum in the capital displays objects from many Mesoamerican cultures, whereas the archaeological site allows you to see the original layout and monumental buildings of an ancient city.

## Tickets, visiting rules and comfortable shoes

Teotihuacan has official INAH rules, a dedicated admission procedure and set visiting hours. According to the institute, the area open to visitors covers hundreds of hectares, so comfortable shoes, water and sun protection are essential. Climbing some structures may be restricted for conservation reasons; do not expect unrestricted access to pyramid summits.

In Mexico City, visiting museums and buildings depends on their opening hours. In particular, **the National Museum of Anthropology is closed on Mondays**. This is an important reason to check dates and the order of the itinerary when booking a city excursion.

Tickets included in different excursions are not identical. Do not assume that museum admission, entry to Teotihuacan and access to every historic building have all been paid for in each option.

For a broader selection, see [Mexico excursions](/mexico/excursion/) and [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/). Details about the ancient city are available on the [Teotihuacan page](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/); this catalog helps you choose the right visiting format.

## Frequently asked questions about Mexico City and Teotihuacan excursions

### Is Teotihuacan located within Mexico City?

No. It is a separate archaeological site in the State of Mexico, requiring a road trip from the capital.

### Can I see Teotihuacan and the anthropology museum on one ready-made excursion?

They are offered as separate excursions. A combined schedule must be agreed specifically rather than assumed from the catalog title.

### How long does the Teotihuacan and Guadalupe excursion take?

The [product page](/mexico/teotihuacan/teotihuacan-guadalupe-tour/) specifies **10 hours**, including transport, guiding and archaeological-site admission.

### Should I plan the anthropology museum for a Monday?

When choosing a city excursion, remember that the museum is closed on Mondays. Confirm the current schedule and choose another date or alternative city tour.
